blocks.text: The chapter contrasts repeated priestly entry and sacrifice with Christ’s single appearance and offering. Its closing movement emphasizes that Christ appears once to deal with sin, has been offered once to bear sins, and will appear again for those awaiting salvation.

The chapter’s description of the earthly sanctuary and a heavenly reality is rhetorical and typological: it develops a comparison for its argument rather than supplying a complete floor plan of heaven. Likewise, its presentation of tabernacle service selects scriptural features to make that argument and should not be read as a neutral description of all Israelite worship or temple practice.

In verses 15–17, the word translated “covenant” may also carry associations of a testament or will. The chapter develops this word alongside death and inheritance language, so the translation question belongs to the local flow of the argument rather than being resolved by one English equivalent alone.

The chapter’s blood language draws together sacrifice, covenant, purification, life, death, and access imagery; no single modern explanation exhausts it. Its language of cleansing the conscience and making worshippers perfect concerns cultic and relational access in context, not necessarily later ideas of psychological perfection.

Hebrews offers a later scriptural interpretation with its own rhetorical argument. Its sanctuary comparison should not be used to make Israelite worship meaningless or to justify contempt for Jewish worship; Christian readings through Hebrews should also be distinguished from the instructions given within Leviticus itself.

Papyrus 46 is an early substantial manuscript witness to Hebrews, though it has gaps and its date can only be estimated paleographically. This is part of the manuscript history through which the whole work, including its sanctuary comparison, has been preserved.
